after.problem:
Let $V={R}_{2}[t]$ be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most $2,$ equipped with the inner product

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=x(1)y(1)+x(2)y(2)+x(3)y(3).
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $p(t)=10-2{t}^{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $p(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $p(t)=10-2{t}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
p(1)=8,\,p(2)=2,\,p(3)=-8.
$$

Computing $‖p(t)‖$ using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖ & =\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{p(1)p(1)+p(2)p(2)+p(3)p(3)} \\  & =\sqrt{[p(1)]^{2}+[p(2)]^{2}+[p(3)]^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(8)^{2}+(2)^{2}+(-8)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{64+4+64} \\  & =\sqrt{132} \\  & =2\sqrt{33}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Let $V=C[0,\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$
after.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2}){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(\pi -\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi }{2})-(0-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{2}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we made use of the trigonometric identities

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t=1\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2t=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖f(t)‖ & =\sqrt{\pi }.\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector in an Inner Product Space of Continuous Functions
content.problem:
Let $V=C[0,\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$
content.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2}){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(\pi -\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi }{2})-(0-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{2}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we made use of the trigonometric identities

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t=1\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2t=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖f(t)‖ & =\sqrt{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector in an Inner Product Space of Continuous Functions
content.problem:
Let $V=C[-1,1]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[-1,1],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)={t}^{2}+1.$
content.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({t}^{2}+1)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}+\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}+t)|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{5}+\frac{2}{3}+1)-(-\frac{1}{5}-\frac{2}{3}-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{3}+2 \\  & =\frac{56}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{\frac{56}{15}}=2\sqrt{\frac{14}{15}}.
$$

after.problem:
Let $V={R}_{2}[t]$ be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most $2,$ equipped with the inner product

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=x(1)y(1)+x(2)y(2)+x(3)y(3).\end{aligned}
$$

Normalize the  vector  $p(t)={t}^{2}-3t+4.$
after.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $p(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖p(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩}.
$$

Since $p(t)={t}^{2}-3t+4,$ we obtain

$$
p(1)=2,\,p(2)=2,\,p(3)=4
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨p(t),p(t)⟩ & =[p(1)]^{2}+[p(2)]^{2}+[p(3)]^{2} \\  & ={2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{4}^{2} \\  & =4+4+16 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖ & =\sqrt{24}=2\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $p(t)$, we divide $p(t)$ by its norm $‖p(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\frac{p(t)}{‖p(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}-3t+4}{2\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{12}({t}^{2}-3t+4)\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Normalizing a Vector in an Inner Product Space
content.problem:
Let $V={R}_{2}[t]$ be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most $2,$ equipped with the inner product

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=x(1)y(1)+x(2)y(2)+x(3)y(3).\end{aligned}
$$

Normalize the  vector  $p(t)={t}^{2}-3t+4.$
content.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $p(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖p(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩}.
$$

Since $p(t)={t}^{2}-3t+4,$ we obtain

$$
p(1)=2,\,p(2)=2,\,p(3)=4
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨p(t),p(t)⟩ & =[p(1)]^{2}+[p(2)]^{2}+[p(3)]^{2} \\  & ={2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{4}^{2} \\  & =4+4+16 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖ & =\sqrt{24}=2\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $p(t)$, we divide $p(t)$ by its norm $‖p(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\frac{p(t)}{‖p(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}-3t+4}{2\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{12}({t}^{2}-3t+4)\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨v,v⟩ & =2\cdot 2+3\cdot 1\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot (-1) \\  & =4+3+1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $v$, we divide $v$ by its norm $‖v‖:$

$$

content.problem:
An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is defined as $⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+3{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ 

Normalize the  vector  $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ under this inner product.
content.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨v,v⟩ & =2\cdot 2+3\cdot 1\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot (-1) \\  & =4+3+1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $v$, we divide $v$ by its norm $‖v‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{v}{‖v‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
